1. REGULATORY ANSWER
Under 21 CFR 312.32(c)(2) as shown in the supplied eCFR text, a sponsor must notify the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) of any unexpected fatal or life-threatening suspected adverse reaction as soon as possible, but in no case later than 7 calendar days after the sponsor's initial receipt of the information (U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Electronic Code of Federal Regulations [eCFR], Title 21, Chapter I, Subchapter D, Part 312, Subpart C, Section 312.32(c)(2); [75 FR 59961, Sept. 29, 2010]; current eCFR version fetched 2026-11-22T23:20:16Z, https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.32).

2. SCOPE: POPULATION, DOSE/EXPOSURE, AND UNITS
- Population: Human subjects/participants exposed to an investigational drug (including clinical trial participants or any other human exposure source, and participants at domestic or foreign study sites in clinical studies of U.S.-marketed drugs conducted under an IND per 21 CFR 312.32(c)(4)).
- Dose or Exposure: Any dose, regimen, or exposure to the investigational drug under an Investigational New Drug (IND) application (or any exposure source from which the sponsor receives safety information regarding the drug under 21 CFR 312.32(c)(1)).
- Units of All Figures: All reporting timeframes in 21 CFR 312.32 are measured in calendar days (specifically 7 calendar days for unexpected fatal or life-threatening suspected adverse reaction notification to FDA, and 15 calendar days for standard IND safety reports, post-investigation determinations, and FDA requests for additional data). In FDA guidance regarding investigator reporting to sponsors under 21 CFR 312.64(b), FDA anticipates initial SAE reporting will generally not exceed 1 calendar day.

3. OPERATIONAL DETAILS FROM THE SUPPLIED REGULATIONS AND GUIDANCE
- Start of the Clock (Day 0): Under 21 CFR 312.32(c)(2) and FDA's guidance for industry Sponsor Responsibilities—Safety Reporting Requirements and Safety Assessment for IND and Bioavailability/Bioequivalence Studies (https://www.fda.gov/media/150356/download, fetched 2026-11-22T23:20:16Z), Day 0 for a 7-calendar-day report is the day the sponsor initially receives the information for a case that is interpretable as a single case.
- Gating Criteria (21 CFR 312.32(c)(1)(i) & (c)(2)): The event must be a suspected adverse reaction (an adverse event for which there is evidence to suggest a causal relationship between the drug and the adverse event), must be unexpected (not listed in the investigator brochure or not listed at the observed specificity or severity, or inconsistent with risk information in the general investigational plan/current IND if an investigator brochure is unavailable, per FDA's IND Safety Reporting webpage), and must be fatal or life-threatening.
- Notification of Participating Investigators (21 CFR 312.32(c)(1)): Under 21 CFR 312.32(c)(1) and Footnote 22 of FDA's December 2025 guidance Investigator Responsibilities – Safety Reporting for Investigational Drugs and Devices (https://www.fda.gov/media/152530/download, fetched 2026-11-22T23:20:16Z), sponsors must also notify all participating investigators (all investigators at U.S. and non-U.S. sites to whom the sponsor provides the drug under any of its INDs or under any investigator's IND) of all serious and unexpected suspected adverse reactions, including fatal or life-threatening ones, in an IND safety report as soon as possible but no later than 15 calendar days after the sponsor determines the information qualifies for reporting.
- Submission Format and Routing (21 CFR 312.32(c)(1)(v) & (c)(3)): Each notification to FDA must prominently identify its contents as an "IND Safety Report" and be transmitted to the responsible review division in the Center for Drug Evaluation and Research (CDER) or the Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research (CBER). An alternative format or frequency may be required by FDA or adopted by the sponsor if agreed to in advance by the director of the responsible FDA review division (21 CFR 312.32(c)(3)). Electronic submission specifications are governed by FDA's Providing Regulatory Submissions in Electronic Format: IND Safety Reports (April 2024) and FDA Regional Implementation Guide for E2B(R3) Electronic Transmission of Individual Case Safety Reports for Drug and Biological Products (April 2024), as referenced in the supplied FDA guidance.
- Investigation, Follow-Up, and Reclassification (21 CFR 312.32(d)): The sponsor must promptly investigate all safety information it receives (312.32(d)(1)). Relevant follow-up information to a 7-calendar-day or 15-calendar-day IND safety report must be submitted as soon as the information is available and labeled "Followup IND Safety Report" (312.32(d)(2)). If an investigation later reveals that an adverse event not initially deemed reportable is reportable under 312.32(c), the sponsor must submit an IND safety report as soon as possible, but in no case later than 15 calendar days after the determination is made (312.32(d)(3)).
- Additional Data Requests (21 CFR 312.32(c)(1)(v)): Upon FDA request, the sponsor must submit any additional data or information deemed necessary as soon as possible, but in no case later than 15 calendar days after receiving the request.
- Non-Admission Disclaimer (21 CFR 312.32(e)): Submitting a safety report does not necessarily reflect a conclusion by the sponsor or FDA that the drug caused or contributed to the adverse event.

### Regulatory Determination: Premarket Notification (510(k)) Submission Lead Time

**Required Submission Lead Time:** **At least 90 days** before the proposed introduction or delivery for introduction of the device into interstate commerce for commercial distribution.

---

### Governing Regulation and Edition Verification
- **Primary Provision:** 21 CFR Part 807, Subpart E, § 807.81(a) (*When a premarket notification submission is required*), 42 FR 42526 (Aug. 23, 1977), as amended at 72 FR 73601 (Dec. 28, 2007) and 89 FR 18792 (Mar. 15, 2024).
- **Version / In-Force Status on 2026-11-21:** Confirmed against the electronic Code of Federal Regulations (eCFR) current text of 21 CFR § 807.81 fetched on 2026-11-22T23:23:35Z (URL: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-H/part-807/subpart-E/section-807.81), the Daily eCFR edition dated 2026-11-12 (https://ecfr.io/Title-21/Part-807/Subpart-E), and the 2025 annual CFR edition (`CFR-2025-title21-vol8-sec807-81.xml`, edition date 2025-04-01). No amendments occurred between March 15, 2024 and November 22, 2026; therefore, the text below reflects the exact regulation in force on 2026-11-21.

---

### Regulatory Scope, Population, and Timing Rule
1. **Regulated Entity and Target Population/Device Scope:** Under 21 CFR § 807.81(a), the requirement applies to each person required to register an establishment pursuant to 21 CFR § 807.20 who proposes to begin the introduction or delivery for introduction into interstate commerce for commercial distribution of a **medical device intended for human use** (no clinical dosing or therapeutic exposure applies; this is a premarket regulatory filing requirement) when any of the following criteria in § 807.81(a)(1)–(3) are met:
   - **First-time commercial distribution of a new device type (§ 807.81(a)(1)):** The device is being introduced into commercial distribution for the first time and is not of the same type as, or not substantially equivalent to, (i) a device in commercial distribution before May 28, 1976, or (ii) a device introduced after May 28, 1976 that was subsequently reclassified into Class I or Class II.
   - **First-time commercial distribution by that registrant (§ 807.81(a)(2)):** The device is being introduced into commercial distribution for the first time by a person required to register under § 807.20, regardless of whether § 807.81(a)(1) applies.
   - **Significant change or modification (§ 807.81(a)(3)):** The device is currently in commercial distribution or is being reintroduced, and is about to be significantly changed or modified in design, components, method of manufacture, or intended use (specifically: (i) a change/modification that could significantly affect safety or effectiveness, such as design, material, chemical composition, energy source, or manufacturing process; or (ii) a major change/modification in intended use).

2. **Mandatory Minimum Lead Time:** Except as provided in 21 CFR § 807.81(b), the premarket notification submission (containing the information specified in 21 CFR § 807.87) must be submitted to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) **at least 90 days** (unit: calendar days) before the proposed introduction or delivery for introduction into interstate commerce for commercial distribution (21 CFR § 807.81(a)).

3. **Statutory/Regulatory Exceptions and Related Deadlines Noted in Subpart E:**
   - **Exceptions under 21 CFR § 807.81(b)(1):** A premarket notification under Subpart E is not required for a device for which (i) a premarket approval application (PMA) under section 515 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act) or a reclassification petition under section 513(f)(2) of the FD&C Act is pending before FDA, or (ii) a predetermined change control plan (PCCP) has been cleared under section 515C of the FD&C Act, provided the change is consistent with that PCCP.
   - **Labeling exception/alternative under 21 CFR § 807.81(b)(2):** For significant modifications under § 807.81(a)(3), the appropriate FDA Center Director may determine that the submission and grant of a written request for an exception or alternative under 21 CFR § 801.128 or § 809.11 satisfies § 807.81(a)(3).
   - **Custom devices (21 CFR § 807.85(a)):** Custom devices within the meaning of section 520(b) of the FD&C Act are exempt from premarket notification requirements under Subpart E.
   - **Radiation-emitting electronic products (21 CFR § 807.81(c)):** Owners or operators of device establishments manufacturing radiation-emitting electronic products (as defined in 21 CFR § 1000.3) must also comply with reporting requirements in 21 CFR Part 1002.
   - **Additional information / resubmission timing (21 CFR Part 807, Subpart E):** If FDA issues a written request for additional information because the original submission lacks sufficient data, the submitter may either submit the requested data or submit a new premarket notification at least **90 days** (unit: days) before intending to market the device (or submit a PMA under section 515); failure to submit additional information within **30 days** (unit: days) of the request results in the submission being considered withdrawn. Separately, under 21 CFR § 807.95(b), where statutory confidentiality conditions apply, FDA will not publicly disclose the existence of a submission for **90 days** (unit: days) from receipt (or **90 days** after receipt of a complete submission following a § 807.87(h) request), and will make a 510(k) summary publicly available within **30 days** (unit: days) after issuing a substantial equivalence determination.

4. **Operational Note:** Submitting at least 90 days prior to proposed commercial distribution satisfies the regulatory filing lead-time mandate in 21 CFR § 807.81(a), which is distinct from FDA's substantive review and clearance determination; the device may not be marketed until FDA issues an order of substantial equivalence or other applicable marketing authorization.

Regulatory Deliverable: IRB/IEC Minimum Membership and Required Composition Characteristics Under ICH E6(R2)

1. Scope, Applicable Population, and Exposure Context
- Governing Guideline: International Council for Harmonisation of Technical Requirements for Pharmaceuticals for Human Use (ICH) Guideline for Good Clinical Practice E6(R2) — Integrated Addendum to ICH E6(R1) (Step 4 adopted November 2016; EMA/CHMP/ICH/135/1995 Step 5 Revision 2; FDA Guidance for Industry).
- Applicable Population: Human subjects involved in clinical trials whose rights, safety, and well-being are protected by an Institutional Review Board (IRB) or Independent Ethics Committee (IEC) (ICH E6(R2), Glossary: Definition of IRB/IEC).
- Dose or Exposure: Not applicable (regulatory committee governance and composition standard rather than a therapeutic intervention).

2. Direct Answers (ICH E6(R2), Section 3.2.1)
Under ICH E6(R2), Section 3.2.1 ('Composition, Functions, and Operations'), the guideline states verbatim:
"3.2.1 The IRB/IEC should consist of a reasonable number of members, who collectively have the qualifications and experience to review and evaluate the science, medical aspects, and ethics of the proposed trial. It is recommended that the IRB/IEC should include:
(a) At least five members.
(b) At least one member whose primary area of interest is in a nonscientific area.
(c) At least one member who is independent of the institution/trial site.
Only those IRB/IEC members who are independent of the investigator and the sponsor of the trial should vote/provide opinion on a trial-related matter.
A list of IRB/IEC members and their qualifications should be maintained."

Accordingly:
- Recommended Minimum Total Membership: 5 members (specifically, "[a]t least five members"; ICH E6(R2), Section 3.2.1(a)).
- Two Membership Characteristics That Should Be Included:
  1. Nonscientific representation: At least 1 member ("[a]t least one member") whose primary area of interest is in a nonscientific area (ICH E6(R2), Section 3.2.1(b)).
  2. Institutional/site independence: At least 1 member ("[a]t least one member") who is independent of the institution/trial site (ICH E6(R2), Section 3.2.1(c)).

3. Complementary Composition, Voting, and Jurisdictional Considerations
- Recommendation vs. Binding Mandate: ICH E6(R2) Section 3.2.1 frames the 5-member floor and the two specific member characteristics using recommendation language ("It is recommended that the IRB/IEC should include..."), while also stating in Section 3.2.2 that the IRB/IEC "should comply with GCP and with the applicable regulatory requirement(s)." Similarly, the ICH E6(R2) Glossary notes that the legal status, composition, function, operations, and regulatory requirements pertaining to IECs may differ among countries, provided the committee acts in agreement with GCP. Reviewing clinicians and regulatory leads must therefore verify applicable national/local regulations (for example, national statutory minimums or quorum rules) in the trial's jurisdiction.
- Collective Qualification and Quorum: Regardless of headcount above the 5-member recommended minimum, the members must collectively possess the qualifications and experience to evaluate the science, medical aspects, and ethics of the proposed trial (ICH E6(R2), Section 3.2.1). Decisions must be made at announced meetings with at least a quorum present as stipulated in the IRB/IEC's written operating procedures (ICH E6(R2), Section 3.2.3), and the IRB/IEC must document its composition (names and qualifications of members) and establishing authority in written procedures (ICH E6(R2), Sections 3.2.1 and 3.3.1).
- Voting and Deliberation Independence: Only IRB/IEC members who are independent of the investigator and the sponsor of the trial should vote or provide an opinion on a trial-related matter (ICH E6(R2), Section 3.2.1), and only members who participate in the IRB/IEC review and discussion should vote/provide opinion and/or advice (ICH E6(R2), Section 3.2.4). While the investigator may provide information on any aspect of the trial, the investigator should not participate in IRB/IEC deliberations or voting (ICH E6(R2), Section 3.2.5). Nonmembers with expertise in special areas may be invited for assistance (ICH E6(R2), Section 3.2.6).
- Version Note (ICH E6(R3) Continuity): For reference only (outside the ICH E6(R2) constraint of this request), the subsequent ICH E6(R3) Step 4 Final Consolidated Guideline (Section 1.3.1) retains the recommendation of at least 5 members and at least 1 independent member, while updating the nonscientific characteristic wording from "nonscientific area" to "not in medical sciences."

4. Full Citations

ICH Guideline for Good Clinical Practice E6(R2), Step 5 Revision 2 (EMA/CHMP/ICH/135/1995), Section 3.2.1–3.2.6, Section 3.3.1, and Glossary. https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/documents/scientific-guideline/ich-guideline-good-clinical-practice-e6r2-step-5-revision-2_en.pdf

- International Council for Harmonisation (ICH). 1. REGULATORY DETERMINATION
Under 21 CFR Part 814 as in force on 2026-11-21, the legacy HDE checklist must replace the obsolete ceiling of 4,000 individuals per year with a prevalence ceiling of not more than 8,000 (<= 8,000) individuals in the United States per year (21 CFR § 814.3(n); 21 CFR § 814.100(b), eCFR current as of 2026-11-22T23:30:01Z; 2025 CFR Title 21, Vol. 8, Part 814).

2. STATUTORY AND REGULATORY BASIS (WITH VERSION CITATIONS)
- Definition of HUD (21 CFR § 814.3(n), eCFR Title 21, Part 814, fetched 2026-11-22T23:30:01Z): "HUD (humanitarian use device) means a medical device intended to benefit patients in the treatment or diagnosis of a disease or condition that affects or is manifested in not more than 8,000 individuals in the United States per year."
- Purpose and Scope of Subpart H (21 CFR § 814.100(b), 61 FR 33244, June 26, 1996, as amended through 82 FR 26349, June 7, 2017, and 85 FR 18442, Apr. 2, 2020; eCFR fetched 2026-11-22T23:30:01Z): Implements sections 515A and 520(m) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act to encourage discovery and use of devices intended to benefit patients in the treatment or diagnosis of diseases or conditions that affect or are manifested in not more than 8,000 individuals in the United States per year.
- Statutory Amendment (Section 3052, 21st Century Cures Act, Pub. L. No. 114-255, Dec. 13, 2016; FDA Humanitarian Use Device (HUD) Designation Program, accessed 2026-11-22T23:30:01Z): Raised the HUD qualifying population estimate from "fewer than 4,000" to "not more than 8,000" individuals in the United States per year (codified in 21 CFR Part 814 via 82 FR 26349, June 7, 2017).
- Correction to Project Assumptions: Note that the exact regulatory boundary is "not more than 8,000" (inclusive, <= 8,000 individuals in the United States per year), rather than "fewer than 8,000," and the governing HUD definition citations are 21 CFR § 814.3(n) and § 814.100(b) (alongside § 814.102(a)(5)), rather than § 814.100(a)(2).

3. READY-TO-APPLY HDE CHECKLIST UPDATE TEXT
Replace any checklist item quoting "4,000" or "fewer than 4,000" with the following updated items:

- Checklist Item A — HUD Population Prevalence Ceiling (Treatment or Diagnosis):
  "Verify that the medical device is intended to benefit patients in the treatment or diagnosis of a disease or condition that affects or is manifested in not more than 8,000 (<= 8,000) individuals in the United States per year, supported by appended authoritative references (e.g., specialized medical journal citations, textbooks, specialized medical society proceedings, governmental statistics publications, or credible research/survey conclusions if literature does not exist)." [Source: 21 CFR § 814.3(n), § 814.100(b), § 814.102(a)(5), eCFR current as of 2026-11-21]

- Checklist Item B — Additional Diagnostic Device Exposure Ceiling:
  "If the device is intended for diagnostic purposes, verify documentation demonstrating that not more than 8,000 (<= 8,000) patients in the United States per year would be subjected to diagnosis using the device (device exposure ceiling)." [Source: 21 CFR § 814.102(a)(5), § 814.102(b)(3)(ii), eCFR current as of 2026-11-21]

- Checklist Item C — Medically Plausible Subset (Orphan Subset) Criterion:
  "If the proposed indication represents a subset of a non-rare/common disease or condition, verify documentation demonstrating that the defined patient population is a medically plausible subset ('orphan subset') based on an intrinsic feature of the device (e.g., adverse event profile or mode of action) making use inappropriate in the remaining population, rather than clinical study inclusion/exclusion criteria or unmet need alone." [Source: 21 CFR § 814.102(a)(3), § 814.102(b)(3)(iii); FDA HUD Designation Program, accessed 2026-11-22]

- Checklist Item D — Post-Approval Periodic Reporting Threshold (Related Threshold Check):
  "For post-approval HDE periodic reports, verify tracking of the number of devices shipped or sold since initial marketing approval; if the number shipped or sold exceeds 8,000 devices, verify inclusion of an explanation and estimate of the number of devices used per patient (and, if a single device is used on multiple patients, an estimate of the number of patients treated or diagnosed with the device and the basis for the estimate)." [Source: 21 CFR § 814.126(b)(1)(iii), eCFR current as of 2026-11-21]

4. POPULATION COUNTING AND UNITS CLARIFICATION
- Population: Individuals in the United States (all ages, with pediatric subpopulations—neonates, infants, children, adolescents, defined as 21 years of age or younger at diagnosis or treatment under 21 CFR § 814.3(s)—separately documented under 21 CFR § 814.100(c)).
- Metric and Units: Annual U.S. disease/condition prevalence ("not more than 8,000 individuals in the United States per year"), not total devices sold. For diagnostic devices specifically, both disease prevalence (<= 8,000 individuals in the United States per year) and annual U.S. diagnostic exposure (<= 8,000 patients in the United States subjected to diagnosis by the device per year) must be satisfied (21 CFR § 814.102(a)(5), § 814.102(b)(3)(i)–(ii)).

1. Summary Answers
- When the tuberculin skin test (TST) reaction must be examined: 48–72 hours after administration (placement) [CDC, Clinical Testing and Diagnosis for Tuberculosis, Apr. 17, 2025; CDC, Clinical Testing Guidance for Tuberculosis: Tuberculin Skin Test, Jan. 31, 2025]. If a patient does not return within 72 hours, they must be rescheduled for another skin test [CDC, Tuberculin Skin Testing Information for Health Care Providers].
- Who must examine it: A trained health care worker (also referred to in the interpretation section as a trained health care professional or designated, trained health care provider) [CDC, Clinical Testing and Diagnosis for Tuberculosis, Apr. 17, 2025; CDC, Clinical Testing Guidance for Tuberculosis: Tuberculin Skin Test, Jan. 31, 2025]. Because authorization varies by jurisdiction, providers should consult state and local public health authorities to determine who is authorized to place and read TB skin tests in their state [CDC, Clinical Testing and Diagnosis for Tuberculosis, Apr. 17, 2025; CDC, Clinical Testing Guidance for Tuberculosis: Tuberculin Skin Test, Jan. 31, 2025].

2. Clinical Context, Population, and Exposure
- Population: CDC recommends testing people who are at increased risk for tuberculosis (TB) infection [CDC, Clinical Testing and Diagnosis for Tuberculosis, Apr. 17, 2025]. ### Regulatory Time Limits for a De Novo Request Accepted Without Additional-Information Submission
Under **21 CFR Part 860, Subpart D (De Novo Classification)**, as in force on **2026-11-21** (verified against the eCFR current as fetched 2026-11-22T23:45:13Z; 86 FR 54846–54847, Oct. 5, 2021, with 21 CFR § 860.240 amended at 90 FR 55980, Dec. 4, 2025):

1. **Outside Time Limit for Acceptance Notification: 15 days**
   - **Figure and Unit:** `15 days` (the regulation uses "days" without specifying business or working days, corresponding to calendar days).
   - **Trigger / Clock Start:** Date the De Novo request is received by FDA.
   - **Governing Provision:** **21 CFR § 860.230(a)–(b)** (*Accepting a De Novo request*, eCFR current as of 2026-11-22; editorial note citing 73 FR 35341, June 23, 2008, and 86 FR 54846, Oct. 5, 2021).
   - **Regulatory Requirement:** Under § 860.230(a), within **15 days** after a De Novo request is received by FDA, FDA must notify the requester whether the De Novo request has been accepted (i.e., that FDA has made a threshold determination that the submission contains the information necessary to permit substantive review). Under § 860.230(b), if FDA does not find that any refusal-to-accept grounds in § 860.230(c)(1) apply—or if FDA fails to complete the acceptance review within **15 days**—FDA will accept the De Novo request for review and notify the requester. The notice includes the De Novo request reference number and the date of acceptance, which is the date the accepted De Novo request was received by FDA.

2. **Outside Time Limit for FDA's Substantive Review and Granting or Declining Order: 120 days**
   - **Figure and Unit:** `120 days` (stated as "days" in the regulation).
   - **Trigger / Clock Start:** Date of FDA's receipt of the De Novo request (because the request is accepted without any additional-information submission under § 860.230(c)(3)).
   - **Governing Provision:** **21 CFR § 860.240(a)** (*Procedures for review of a De Novo request*, 86 FR 54847, Oct. 5, 2021, as amended at 90 FR 55980, Dec. 4, 2025), cross-referencing **21 CFR § 860.260(a)** (order granting) and **21 CFR § 860.260(b)** (order declining).
   - **Regulatory Requirement:** Under § 860.240(a), FDA begins substantive review after the De Novo request is accepted under § 860.230. Within **120 days** after receipt of the De Novo request (or receipt of additional information resulting in acceptance under § 860.230, which does not apply here), FDA will review the De Novo request and send the requester an order granting the De Novo request under § 860.260(a) or an order declining the De Novo request under § 860.260(b).
   - **Important Clock Relationship:** The **120-day** limit is measured from FDA's receipt of the original De Novo request—not 120 days added on top of the 15-day acceptance period—consistent with § 860.230(b), which sets the acceptance date as the receipt date.

### Scope and Contextual Notes from 21 CFR Part 860, Subpart D
- **Acceptance Without Additional-Information Submission:** Because the request is accepted on the initial filing without a refusal-to-accept under § 860.230(c)(1)–(2) and without an additional-information submission under § 860.230(c)(3), the alternative acceptance-date and review-clock-start rules triggered by receipt of acceptance-stage additional information do not apply.
- **Substantive-Review Interactions:** During substantive review, 21 CFR § 860.240(b) permits the requester to supplement or amend a pending De Novo request and authorizes FDA to require additional information necessary to complete review (§ 860.240(b)(1)); failure to provide a complete response to a § 860.240(b)(1) request within **180 days** after issuance results in deemed withdrawal under **21 CFR § 860.250(a)(1)**. Additionally, under § 860.240(c) (as amended at 90 FR 55980, Dec. 4, 2025), FDA may inspect relevant facilities prior to granting or declining the request to verify clinical/nonclinical data collection integrity or Quality Management System Regulation (21 CFR Part 820) compliance. The scenario analyzed here assumes no post-acceptance additional-information submission or withdrawal occurs, leaving the statutory/regulatory outside limits in § 860.230(a)–(b) and § 860.240(a) at **15 days** and **120 days**, respectively.

REGULATORY DETERMINATION: PREMARKET NOTIFICATION (510(k)) EXEMPTION FOR CUSTOM DEVICES

Disclaimer: This output is a draft regulatory analysis for review by a qualified clinician and regulatory affairs professional. It is not medical advice and is not intended for direct patient care.

1. Verdict
No. Under 21 CFR Part 807 Subpart E as in force on 2026-11-21, a manufacturer of a device that meets the custom-device meaning in section 520(b) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act) is NOT required to submit a premarket notification (510(k)) at least 90 days before introducing or delivering the device into interstate commerce for commercial distribution, provided the conditions of 21 CFR 807.85(a) are satisfied.

2. Applicability Scope (Population, Exposure, and Jurisdictional Parameters)
- Target Population: Individual U.S. human patients named in the order of a physician, dentist, or other specially qualified person, or individual physicians, dentists, or other specially qualified persons using the device in the course of conducting their practice for a special need (21 CFR 807.85(a)(1)–(2); FD&C Act section 520(b)).
- Exposure / Regulatory Event: Introduction or delivery for introduction into U.S. interstate commerce for commercial distribution of a medical device intended for human use (21 CFR 807.81(a)).
- Evaluation Date: Regulatory text in force on 2026-11-21 (verified against eCFR fetched 2026-11-22T23:52:49Z and 2025 CFR Title 21, Volume 8).

3. Governing Regulations and Detailed Regulatory Analysis
- General Premarket Notification Rule (21 CFR 807.81(a); 42 FR 42526, Aug. 23, 1977, as amended at 72 FR 73601, Dec. 28, 2007; 89 FR 18792, Mar. 15, 2024): Each person required to register an establishment under 21 CFR 807.20 must submit a premarket notification to the FDA at least 90 days (time unit: days) before proposing to begin the introduction or delivery for introduction into interstate commerce for commercial distribution of a device intended for human use that is being introduced for the first time (not of the same type as, or substantially equivalent to, a device in commercial distribution before May 28, 1976, or reclassified into Class I or II thereafter), being introduced for the first time by that registrant, or undergoing a significant change or modification in design, components, method of manufacture, or intended use (unless an exception in 21 CFR 807.81(b) applies, such as a pending premarket approval application, reclassification petition, or cleared predetermined change control plan).
- Custom Device Exemption (21 CFR 807.85(a); 42 FR 42526, Aug. 23, 1977, as amended at 81 FR 70340, Oct. 12, 2016): Notwithstanding the 90-day requirement in 21 CFR 807.81(a), 21 CFR 807.85(a) explicitly provides that a custom device is exempt from the premarket notification requirements of 21 CFR Part 807 Subpart E if the device is within the meaning of section 520(b) of the FD&C Act, and:
  (1) It is intended for use by a patient named in the order of the physician or dentist (or other specially qualified person); OR
  (2) It is intended solely for use by a physician or dentist (or other specially qualified person) and is not generally available to, or generally used by, other physicians or dentists (or other specially qualified persons).
- Statutory Alignment (FD&C Act Section 520(b); FDA Custom Device Exemption Program Reference, https://www.fda.gov/media/89996/download, fetched 2026-11-22T23:52:49Z): A device within the meaning of section 520(b) necessarily deviates from premarket requirements because it is sufficiently unique that clinical investigations would be impractical and could not be performed to demonstrate conformance to applicable performance standards or support premarket review; it is made upon the written request of a physician or dentist to treat a unique pathology/physiological condition (patient-centric) or meet a special practice need (physician-centric), is not generally available in the United States in finished form, and orders are not solicited by the firm. Personalized or patient-fitted devices (devices legally marketed in a form modified prior to use in each patient, such as a milled dental abutment blank or patient-fitted 3D-printed orthopedic device where a conventional device is cleared) are NOT custom devices and do not qualify for this exemption.

4. Continuing Regulatory Obligations (Non-Exempt Requirements)
Although exempt from 90-day premarket notification under 21 CFR 807.85(a) and from performance standards and premarket approval (sections 514 and 515 of the FD&C Act), a custom device remains subject to applicable post-market and general controls per FDA's Custom Device Exemption Program requirements (https://www.fda.gov/media/89996/download):
- Quality System Regulation: 21 CFR Part 820 (custom devices are not exempt).
- Establishment Registration and Device Listing: 21 CFR Part 807 (registration and listing requirements still apply).
- Labeling: 21 CFR Part 801 (must provide adequate directions for use and must not be false or misleading).
- Medical Device Reporting (Adverse Event Reporting): 21 CFR Part 803.
- Corrections and Removals: 21 CFR Part 806.
- Custom Device Justification Documentation / Reporting: Documentation supporting patient-centric or physician-centric custom-device status, including device description, manufacturing/assembly details, justification of deviation from premarket requirements, statement of non-general availability, and patient/physician identifiers or special practice need statements.

- Current NICE guideline covering the scope (Ask 1): NICE guideline NG136 (Hypertension in adults: diagnosis and management; published 28 August 2019; last updated and last reviewed 26 February 2026, with a minor amendment logged October 2026 in the update history).
- Earlier NICE hypertension guideline updated and replaced (Ask 2): NICE guideline CG127.
- Additional supersession for type 2 diabetes: NG136 also updates and replaces the section on diagnosing and managing hypertension (section 1.4 / section 1.44 blood pressure management) previously contained in NICE guideline NG28 (Type 2 diabetes in adults: management; published 02 December 2015; last updated 18 February 2026; last reviewed 05 November 2026).

2. Scope, Population, and Supersession Lineage
- Population and exposure/intervention scope: Per NG136 (Overview and Recommendations), the guideline covers identifying and treating primary hypertension (measuring blood pressure, diagnosing hypertension, assessing cardiovascular risk and target organ damage, lifestyle interventions, starting antihypertensive drug treatment, monitoring treatment and blood pressure targets, and choosing antihypertensive drug treatment steps 1 to 4) in adults aged 18 years and over (population: >=18 years), explicitly including adults with type 2 diabetes.
- Direct replacement statement (NG136 Overview): "This guideline updates and replaces NICE guideline CG127. It also updates and replaces the section on blood pressure management in the NICE guideline on type 2 diabetes in adults (NG28)."
- Corroboration in NG28 (Section 1.44 and Update Information, August 2019 entry): Recommendations on diagnosing and managing hypertension were removed from NG28 and cross-referenced to NG136 because diagnosis, treatment, and monitoring of hypertension are broadly the same for adults aged 18 years and over with type 2 diabetes as for other adults, with diabetes-specific variations detailed within NG136 (for example: annual blood pressure measurement in adults with type 2 diabetes without previously diagnosed hypertension or renal disease [Rec 1.2.12]; checking for postural hypotension in adults with hypertension and type 2 diabetes [Rec 1.4.16]; and reviewing existing antihypertensive drug treatment when type 2 diabetes is diagnosed [Rec 1.4.25]).
- Note on drug doses/exposures: No specific pharmacological agent doses are evaluated in this guideline-identification summary; any pathway section covering antihypertensive steps 1 to 4 must specify drug, dose, and units per NG136 and relevant product labels.

3. Key Quantitative Thresholds and Scope Boundaries in NG136 (Cited with Population and Units)
- Clinic blood pressure targets (NG136 Tables 1 and 2):
  * Adults aged under 80 years with hypertension (with or without type 2 diabetes): target below 140/90 mmHg (Rec 1.4.20).
  * Adults aged 80 years and over with hypertension (with or without type 2 diabetes): target below 150/90 mmHg (Rec 1.4.21).
  * Note on units in Tables 1 and 2: Numeric targets (140/90 and 150/90) are stated in mmHg (consistent with standard clinic blood pressure units and NG136 Rec 1.5.1 threshold of 180/120 mmHg or more for same-day specialist referral assessment when no target organ damage is present).
- Cross-guideline boundaries where treatment differs (NG136 Recommendations, Table 1, and Update Information):
  * Chronic kidney disease (CKD) or type 1 diabetes with albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR) less than 70 mg/mmol in adults aged under 80 years: clinic target below 140/90 mmHg (per NICE guidelines on CKD [Rec 1.6.1] and type 1 diabetes in adults [Rec 1.13.8]).
  * CKD or type 1 diabetes with ACR of 70 mg/mmol or more in adults aged under 80 years: clinic target below 130/80 mmHg (per NICE guidelines on CKD [Rec 1.6.2] and type 1 diabetes in adults [Rec 1.13.8]).
  * Hypertension in pregnancy and secondary causes of hypertension (Rec 1.2.13): Pathway must signpost to NICE's guideline on hypertension in pregnancy and specialist investigations where clinically indicated.

4. Guideline Currency, Evidence Gaps, and Documentation Nuances
- Currency and ongoing surveillance: NG136 states "Published: 28 August 2019" and "Last updated: 26 February 2026" (adding Rec 1.2.11 on healthy living advice for people with raised blood pressure not diagnosed with hypertension). Notably, the Update Information page also records an "October 2026" minor amendment to Rec 1.4.26 clarifying when to apply NG136 versus the CKD guideline, even though the page header still displays 26 February 2026; pathway authors should verify the latest PDF/web release date at final sign-off.
- Thin or evolving evidence flagged by NICE: NG136 explicitly notes that evidence is currently under monitoring regarding differential responses to antihypertensive drugs across ethnic groups and states NICE will decide whether to update recommendations once ongoing research is published. DRAFT REGULATORY ANALYSIS FOR QUALIFIED CLINICIAN REVIEW — NOT MEDICAL OR LEGAL ADVICE AND NOT FOR PATIENT CARE.

1. Scope, Population, and Exposure
- Population: Human subjects eligible for enrollment in an FDA-regulated clinical investigation as defined in 21 CFR § 50.3(c) (eCFR Title 21, Part 50, accessed 2026-11-23), including general adult populations, children as defined in 21 CFR § 50.3 and governed by 21 CFR Part 50 Subpart D (66 FR 20598, Apr. 24, 2001, as amended at 78 FR 12951, Feb. 26, 2013), and subjects in life-threatening emergencies governed by 21 CFR § 50.24.
- Dose or Exposure: Not applicable to a specific investigational product; this regulatory assessment applies generically to any experiment involving an FDA-regulated test article and 1 or more human subjects subject to prior submission under section 505(i) or 520(g) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act or intended for submission to/inspection by FDA (21 CFR § 50.3(c)).
- Regulatory Baseline Date: 21 CFR Part 50 as in force on 2026-11-21 (verified against eCFR current text fetched 2026-11-23).

2. Verdict (Ask 2): Is Minimal Risk Alone Sufficient to Enroll Without Informed Consent?
No. Under 21 CFR Part 50 as in force on 2026-11-21, the fact that a clinical investigation involves no more than minimal risk is NOT sufficient on its own for an investigator to enroll a person without informed consent.

First, an investigator cannot unilaterally waive informed consent; only the responsible Institutional Review Board (IRB) may approve a consent waiver or alteration after making and documenting specific regulatory findings (21 CFR § 50.22; 88 FR 88248, Dec. 21, 2023).

Second, under 21 CFR § 50.22 ("Exception from informed consent requirements for minimal risk clinical investigations," 88 FR 88248, Dec. 21, 2023), minimal risk is only 1 of 5 required criteria (4 criteria if identifiable private information or identifiable biospecimens are not used). Specifically, the IRB responsible for the review, approval, and continuing review of the clinical investigation may approve an informed consent procedure that omits or alters some or all elements of informed consent in 21 CFR § 50.25(a) and (b), or waive the requirement to obtain informed consent, only if the IRB finds and documents ALL of the following:
- (a) Minimal Risk: "The clinical investigation involves no more than minimal risk to the subjects" (21 CFR § 50.22(a));
- (b) Impracticability of Research: "The clinical investigation could not practicably be carried out without the requested waiver or alteration" (21 CFR § 50.22(b));
- (c) Impracticability Regarding Identifiable Data/Biospecimens: "If the clinical investigation involves using identifiable private information or identifiable biospecimens, the clinical investigation could not practicably be carried out without using such information or biospecimens in an identifiable format" (21 CFR § 50.22(c));
- (d) Rights and Welfare: "The waiver or alteration will not adversely affect the rights and welfare of the subjects" (21 CFR § 50.22(d)); and
- (e) Post-Participation Information: "Whenever appropriate, the subjects or legally authorized representatives will be provided with additional pertinent information after participation" (21 CFR § 50.22(e)).

Third, additional or distinct requirements apply to special populations and contexts:
- Children (21 CFR Part 50, Subpart D): Children are persons who have not attained the legal age for consent to treatments or procedures involved in clinical investigations under applicable local law (21 CFR § 50.3). Under 21 CFR § 50.51 (78 FR 12951, Feb. 26, 2013), a clinical investigation presenting no greater than minimal risk to children may involve children only if the IRB finds both that no greater than minimal risk is presented (§ 50.51(a)) and that adequate provisions are made for soliciting child assent and parental/guardian permission as set forth in § 50.55 (§ 50.51(b)). Parental/guardian permission is required in accordance with and to the extent that consent is required under Part 50 (§ 50.55(e)), with permission of 1 parent sufficient for investigations under § 50.51 or § 50.52 (§ 50.55(e)(1)) and 2 parents required under § 50.53 or § 50.54 unless an exception in § 50.55(e)(2) applies. Even for waiving child assent alone (when children are capable of assenting), the IRB must find and document 4 criteria under 21 CFR § 50.55(d)(1)–(4): minimal risk, no adverse effect on rights and welfare, impracticability without the waiver, and post-participation information whenever appropriate.
- Emergency Research (21 CFR § 50.24): The Part 50 emergency research exception from informed consent is not triggered by minimal risk; instead, it requires a life-threatening situation with unproven or unsatisfactory available treatments, infeasibility of consent, prospect of direct benefit, impracticability without the waiver, concurrence of a non-participating licensed physician IRB member/consultant, submission under a separate IND or IDE (§ 50.24(d)), post-enrollment notification procedures, and IRB record retention for at least 3 years after completion of the clinical investigation (§ 50.24(c)).

3. Definition of Minimal Risk (Ask 3): How Does 21 CFR Part 50 Define Minimal Risk?
21 CFR § 50.3(k) (eCFR Title 21, Part 50, § 50.3, fetched 2026-11-23) defines minimal risk verbatim as:
"Minimal risk means that the probability and magnitude of harm or discomfort anticipated in the research are not greater in and of themselves than those ordinarily encountered in daily life or during the performance of routine physical or psychological examinations or tests."

4. Operational Guidance for Clinical Research Application
If an investigator wishes to enroll subjects without informed consent in a minimal-risk FDA-regulated clinical investigation, the research team must submit a written justification to the responsible IRB demonstrating each applicable criterion in 21 CFR § 50.22(a)–(e) (and 21 CFR Part 50 Subpart D if children are enrolled), rather than relying on minimal risk status alone, and must not enroll any subject without prior IRB approval and documentation of those findings.
